findings_qualitative.value: HBC 494 is resolved into a binary system (HBC 494 N and HBC 494 S) with two individual circumstellar disks and no detected circumbinary disk or internal disk substructures at 30 mas resolution.

evidence.quote: Here, we present follow-up observations at ∼0′′.03, resolving the system into two components: HBC 494 N (primary) and HBC 494 S (secondary). No circumbinary disk was detected.
At 30 mas resolution, no substructures were detected (see the radial profiles in Figure 3).

findings_qualitative.value: At large scales (8000 au), 12CO traces wide-angle (~150 deg) bipolar outflow arcs while 13CO and C18O trace a rotating, infalling, and expanding envelope with a rotation axis nearly perpendicular to the outflow.

evidence.quote: show southern and northern 12 CO wide-angle arcs (∼ 150 ◦ ) and no clear signal of large structures
The 13CO emission traces the rotating, infalling, and expanding envelope surrounding the system, showing a small deviation from the 12CO outflowing arcs’ rotation axis.
It is noticeable that the 13CO emission has a rotation axis almost perpendicular to the 12CO outflows axis, ensuring that the physical processes behind the two are different.

findings_qualitative.value: At small scales (150 au), continuum-subtracted 12CO and 13CO moment 0 maps show cavities/holes at the continuum disk positions and no clear rotational signatures.

evidence.quote: However, by looking at the molecular lines in this scale (see the moment maps in Figure 7, left and middle columns), we could not clearly detect the presence of the disks or their rotational signatures.
Additionally, the area within the continuum disks highlights regions similar to cavities or “holes" (Figure 7, left column, upper and middle row).

claims.hypothesis: The elongation and asymmetry previously observed in the millimeter continuum of HBC 494 at ~0.25 arcsec resolution is caused by an unresolved structure or a secondary disk.
claims.experiment: Observed HBC 494 with ALMA Band 6 at ~0.03 arcsec resolution combining short and long baseline configurations and fitted 2D Gaussians with CASA imfit.
claims.result: Resolved two continuum disks, HBC 494 N (105.2 mJy, 84.0 x 66.9 mas) and HBC 494 S (21.1 mJy, 64.6 x 46.0 mas), separated by 0.18 arcsec (75 au), with no detected substructures or circumbinary disk.
claims.finding: HBC 494 is a binary system where the primary disk is ~5 times brighter/more massive and ~2 times bigger than the secondary disk.

evidence.quote: ALMA Cycle-2 observations in the millimeter continuum (∼0′′.25 angular resolution) show that the disk is elongated with an apparent asymmetry (Cieza et al. 2018), indicating the presence of an unresolved structure or a secondary disk.
Here, we present follow-up observations at ∼0′′.03, resolving the system into two components: HBC 494 N (primary) and HBC 494 S (secondary). No circumbinary disk was detected.
The observations show that the primary is ∼5 times brighter/more massive and ∼2 times bigger than the secondary.

claims.hypothesis: Eruptive YSO disks (FUors/EXors) are more massive than typical Class 0/I disks, and disks in multiple systems are smaller than those in single systems due to dynamical interactions.
claims.experiment: Calculated dust masses (assuming T=20 K and optically thin emission) and deconvolved FWHM/2 radii for HBC 494 N and S and compared them against literature samples of resolved FUors, EXors, and Class 0/I disks.
claims.result: HBC 494 N has M_dust = 1.43 M_Jup (comparable to FUors) and HBC 494 S has M_dust = 0.29 M_Jup (comparable to EXors); both disks are smaller than single eruptive YSO disks.
claims.finding: HBC 494 disks preserve high masses typical of eruptive systems while their sizes are smaller than single eruptive YSOs, consistent with tidal truncation and dynamical evolution in multiple systems.

evidence.quote: We notice that the northern component has a similar mass to the FUors, while the southern has to EXors. The HBC 494 disks show individual sizes that are smaller than single eruptive YSOs.

A clear difference is seen when we compare the disks from multiple systems (hexagon symbols) and single systems. The latter present bigger sizes as they are not targets for tidal truncation, enhanced radial drift, and more aggressive photoevaporation

claims.hypothesis: Close-separation binary systems like HBC 494 form via rotational disk fragmentation, which produces spin-aligned and coplanar disks, rather than direct/turbulent core fragmentation.
claims.experiment: Derived the inclinations and position angles of HBC 494 N and HBC 494 S from 2D Gaussian fits to the continuum emission and compared their relative orientations.
claims.result: The disks have very similar inclinations (Delta i = 7.5 ± 4.1 deg) and position angles (Delta PA = 4.6 ± 7.0 deg).
claims.finding: The HBC 494 disks are in a quasi-coplanar, spin-aligned configuration, tentatively suggesting formation by rotational disk fragmentation, though small-scale gas kinematics and astrometry are needed to confirm.

evidence.quote: The HBC 494 disks have similar inclinations (Δ𝑖 = 7.5 ± 4.1 degrees) and similar PAs (Δ𝑃𝐴 = 4.6 ± 7.0 degrees). The relative orientations of the disks suggest that the system is coplanar.

Thus, we tentatively suggest that HBC 494 was formed by rotational disk fragmentation rather than direct collapsing. However, more precise observation of the kinematics of the surrounding gas on a small scale (Vorobyov et al. 2021), complemented with orbital information coming from astrometrical measurements, is required to evaluate this hypothesis.

claims.hypothesis: Cavities observed in the small-scale continuum-subtracted 12CO and 13CO moment 0 maps within the continuum disk areas trace either physical gas removal/chemical destruction by jets/radiation or an artifact of continuum over-subtraction due to optically thick lines.
claims.experiment: Produced small-scale CO moment 0 maps and spatial profiles along the disk semi-major axes before and after uvcontsub continuum subtraction.
claims.result: Spatial profiles show that continuum overestimation due to foreground optically thick line absorption propagated through uvcontsub, creating cavities at the continuum peak positions.
claims.finding: The cavities in the small-scale 12CO and 13CO moment 0 maps may be caused by slow-moving outflows/chemical destruction or by optical depth effects and continuum over-subtraction; optically thinner lines are required to recover the true disk gas signal.

evidence.quote: At a smaller scale, the 12CO and 13CO moment zero maps show cavities within the continuum disks’ area, which may indicate continuum over-subtraction or slow-moving jets and chemical destruction along the line-of-sight.

evidence.loc: APPENDIX A: EFFECTS OF CONTINUUM OVER-SUBTRACTION
evidence.quote: Additionally, the continuum was overestimated by foreground optical depth molecular lines that absorbed continuum emission and then propagated to the uvcontsub CASA task.

evidence.loc: APPENDIX A: EFFECTS OF CONTINUUM OVER-SUBTRACTION
evidence.quote: Thus, optically thinner lines must be used to obtain the real signal of disks in moment 0 and 1 maps.

why_this_data.value: Earlier ALMA Cycle 2 observations at ~0.25 arcsec resolution showed an elongated, asymmetric disk around HBC 494, requiring follow-up at ~0.03 arcsec resolution to resolve the substructure or secondary disk.

evidence.quote: ALMA Cycle-2 observations in the millimeter continuum (∼0′′.25 angular resolution) show that the disk is elongated with an apparent asymmetry (Cieza et al. 2018), indicating the presence of an unresolved structure or a secondary disk. In this work, we present ALMA Cycle 4 observations at ∼0′′.03 angular resolution that reveal the binary nature of the HBC 494 system.

why_this_method.value: Used uvcontsub because unsubtracted line dirty images mimicked gaseous envelopes around the disks without revealing gas dynamic signatures; used deconvolved Gaussian FWHM/2 radii and standard isothermal 20 K optically thin dust mass formula to allow consistent comparison with other ALMA disk surveys.

evidence.quote: After producing a dirty image from the visibilities, we noticed that the emission mimicked the presence of gaseous envelopes around the disks (moment 0 maps, see Figure 1, left column) but no gas dynamic signatures were revealed (moment 1 map, see Figure 1, right column). Therefore, we proceeded to remove the visibility’s continuum contributions by using the CASA task uvcontsub.

The disk sizes were calculated using the deconvolved Gaussian FWHM/2 radius obtained from 2D Gaussian fits. This methodology was also used for other ALMA datasets (e.g., Hales et al. 2020; Tobin et al. 2020). Therefore, it allows a consistent comparison with other disks.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Gravitational instability (GI), infall, or stellar flybys as outburst triggering mechanisms were not supported because no spiral, clumpy, or perturbation features were detected in the dust or gas maps.

evidence.quote: For each HBC 494 disk, no clue of trigger mechanisms was found, since the gas and continuum data did not reveal clear spiral or clumpy features indicating a case of infall or GI (see e.g., Zhu et al. 2012; Kratter & Lodato 2016).

Looking at the dust continuum (Figure 2), CO isotopologues moment maps (Figure 7), and the scattered 12CO emission (Figure 12 of Ruíz-Rodríguez et al. 2017), the hypothesis of stellar flybys is also not encouraged since no trace of perturbation was detected (Cuello et al. 2020, 2023).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Manually adding back lost line signal to correct for continuum over-subtraction was rejected because it would only create fake signal at the noise level.

evidence.loc: APPENDIX A: EFFECTS OF CONTINUUM OVER-SUBTRACTION
evidence.quote: The "holes" or cavities seen in the top-right panel could potentially be diminished by manually adding back some of the lost line signal, but this would only create a fake signal at the level of noise.

limitations_admitted.value: Optically thin dust approximation does not account for optically thick inner disk regions, which can underestimate dust masses, while assuming a fixed 20 K dust temperature can overestimate masses if the dust is warmer.

evidence.quote: However, it is worth mentioning that the optically thin analysis can not take into account the innermost regions of the disk (optically thick). This may lead to an underestimation of the dust masses. Also, an underlying miscalculated dust grain temperature can alter the results, overestimating the masses if the dust is warmer than expected.

limitations_admitted.value: Cloud contamination and optical depth effects mask small-scale disk rotational kinematics, prevent detection of a circumbinary gas disk, and cause continuum over-subtraction in uvcontsub.

evidence.quote: However, no HBC 494 circumbinary gas disk was observed due to cloud contamination and optical depth effects.
The dynamics of both disks in such scales were masked principally by cloud contamination.

limitations_admitted.value: Using only the 12-m main array data filters out extended emission on large scales, which requires combining with ALMA single-dish/ACA data to fully recover.

evidence.loc: APPENDIX B: 12CO, 13CO AND C18O CHANNEL MAPS WITH CONTOURS AND THE EFFECT OF CLOUD CONTAMINATION
evidence.quote: It also shows some significant contours on both horizontal extremes, which can be tracers of the filtered signals using only the main array data. The data partially trace features that, due to their large extension, require a combination of the ALMA main and single dish arrays to recover extended flux emission.

referee_caveats_inferred: In Table 2, the rows labeled 'Major axis (au)' (34.8 and 26.7 au) and 'Minor axis (au)' (27.8 and 19.9 au) actually list the FWHM in au, and the row labeled 'FWHM Radius (au)' repeats 34.8 and 26.7 au, whereas at 414 pc an FWHM of 84.0 mas corresponds to 34.8 au diameter (so FWHM/2 radius R_c is ~17.4 au and ~13.4 au, as plotted in Figure 8).
Assuming T_dust = 20 K for an outbursting FUor object (~250 L_sun) likely overestimates the dust mass significantly compared to radiative transfer models of heated disks.

reproducibility.rediscovery_reason: Public ALMA data (2016.1.00630.S) with a straightforward imaging + CASA imfit + analytical dust mass recipe yielding clear, high-SNR numeric results for the binary separation, disk fluxes, deconvolved sizes, inclinations, and masses.
